content.text: Students build from Lessons 3, 4, and 6 by moving from the idea of a hidden figure and symbolic meaning to the way one anecdote can reveal both teamwork and unfair barriers.
Scientific discovery grows through questions, evidence, and collaboration, but history does not always make every contributor visible.
In the next lesson, students will read Chapter 7 and the poem “Tuskegee” to continue tracing how place, opportunity, and exclusion shaped who could participate in science.
Students practice citing evidence to explain both contribution and obstacle, a must-do move for their hidden innovator research article.

Turn and Talk
Directions:
Turn and talk to discuss your response to the question.
When people work together to solve a difficult problem, what factors can strengthen their teamwork, and what factors can make it more challenging?
“In the office, the women felt equal, but in the cafeteria and the bathrooms, the “Colored” signs were a reminder that some were more equal than others.”
Directions:

The author includes this anecdote to describe the impact of the “Colored” signs at Langley and also to compare contrasting experiences of the Black women at Langley. Turn and talk to a partner about the following question:
What are the two contrasting ideas described in this anecdote?
Work with a partner to write a sentence that tells about two contrasting ideas or events in Chapter 6. Use a contrast word such as

Part A: Key Moments
Directions:
Reread the key moments in Chapter 6 with your partner. As you read, record at least two moments in the 3-Column Chart graphic organizer. Label your columns as indicated:
Column 1: Anecdote or moment
Column 2: How it shows collaboration
Column 3: How it shows segregation or resistance.
Pulse Check
Which statement best explains how the cafeteria sign anecdote develops ideas in Chapter 6?
It is included mainly to prove that cafeteria rules were the most important part of the women’s jobs at Langley.
It is included to show that even while the women collaborated as skilled mathematicians, segregation still shaped their daily lives at Langley.
It is included to show that the women worked separately and did not rely on one another to solve problems.
It is included only to make the chapter more dramatic and does not connect to the author’s larger ideas.
Part B: Author’s Purpose and Point of View
Think-Pair-Share
Directions:
Respond to the questions using evidence from Chapter 6. Then discuss your responses with your partner.
What point of view about teamwork is the author conveying through these moments, and how do the examples support it?
Why does the author include examples of collaboration alongside segregation, and how does this choice support her purpose?
What does the author want readers to understand about how these women succeeded, and how do specific details help convey that message?
How do the author’s choices of details shape the reader’s understanding of NASA at the time?
Reflection
Reflect on your understanding of the author’s purpose and point of view using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in explaining how details in a text reveal the author’s purpose and point of view?
Quick Write
Directions:

For your exit ticket, use at least two specific details from Chapter 6 to explain the author’s point of view about the women of West Computing. Then briefly analyze how Shetterly uses an anecdote or pattern of events to advance that point of view. Be sure to use at least one contrast connector (such as
but, although,
or
however
) in your response
Place students in assigned discussion pairs. Invite them to keep Chapter 6 open.
Turn and Talk
Say these directions:
Turn and talk to discuss the following question.
Ask:
When people work together to solve a difficult problem, what factors can strengthen their teamwork, and what factors can make it more challenging?
Teamwork gets stronger when people share ideas and help each other check mistakes. It gets harder when unfair rules or stereotypes stop some people from being treated with respect.
Teacher Tip

Chapter 6 includes examples of racial segregation in the workplace. Briefly remind students that these practices were unjust, that the class is examining them to understand history accurately, and that discussions should be approached with care and respect.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now, let’s explore how the author develops these ideas in Chapter 6 through the use of anecdotes.
Students will activate prior learning from Lesson 6 and analyze how one anecdote can hold two ideas at once.
Using Contrast Sentences to Hold Two Ideas at Once
Display and read aloud the following anecdote from Chapter 6 that describes the signs that were put up at Langley.
“In the office, the women felt equal, but in the cafeteria and the bathrooms, the “Colored” signs were a reminder that some were more equal than others.”
Say these directions:

The author includes this anecdote to describe the impact of the “Colored” signs at Langley and also to compare contrasting experiences of the Black women at Langley. Turn and talk to a partner about the following question:
Ask:
What are the two contrasting ideas described in this anecdote?
The contrasting ideas are that the women felt equal in the office, but the “Colored” signs in the cafeteria and bathrooms made them feel unequal.
Point out to students that the word “but” is used to connect and contrast both ideas within the anecdote.
Say:

Sometimes readers notice one true idea and stop there, but Chapter 6 pushes us to think more deeply. We can see that the women are highly skilled and collaborate effectively, while also recognizing that segregation continues to shape their workplace. In the sentence from Chapter 6, the word “but” allows both truths to exist together in one sentence.
Say:
Work with a partner to write a sentence that tells about two contrasting ideas or events in Chapter 6. Use a contrast word such as
but,
although, while, or whereas
to show a connection between the ideas
Have a few partners share their sentences with the class.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
We will now use this sentence pattern to track how Chapter 6 anecdotes reveal both teamwork and resistance.
Support students in using sentence patterns that let them explain both collaboration and segregation clearly.
Language Focus:
Contrast connectors
Compound-complex sentence structure
Precision in academic explanation
Before Practice (preparation step—optional)
Students orally say the two ideas separately before combining them into one sentence.
Prompt students away from overusing but by asking which connector better shows timing or contrast.
Emphasize that both sides of the sentence must stay important; one side should not erase the other.
You said they worked together but it was unfair—we can explain that by saying “Although the women collaborated, segregation still shaped their workplace.”
That idea connects to defiance because removing the sign was not just an action; it was resistance to an unfair rule.
Although ___, ___.
This contrast matters because ___.
Invite students to test the sentence orally in the language they think in first and then restate it in English with a partner.
If students write only one side of the contrast → Prompt: “What is the second true idea in this same scene?”
If students misuse although without a complete second clause → Prompt: “Finish the thought after the comma with a full sentence idea.”
Student combines two connected ideas in one sentence with an accurate connector.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Holding Both Ideas in One Sentence

Give students the starter “Although the women ___, the workplace ___” and have them complete each side before rewriting independently. Comma Placement: Have students underline the opening clause and place the comma where the first complete idea ends.
Ready for extension

Write two different sentences about the same anecdote, one with although and one with whereas, and compare how the meaning shifts. Add a final phrase beginning with which shows to explain why the contrast matters.
Students will explore how contrast sentence patterns can be used to compare collaboration and segregation.
Part A: Key Moments (RI.6.3) (15 minutes)
Have students work in pairs with Chapter 6 open. Direct them to read Chapter 6 and record two moments showing the women working together on calculations or problem-solving.
Say these directions:
Reread the key moments in Chapter 6 with your partner. As you read, record at least two moments in the
3-Column Chart
graphic organizer. Label your columns as indicated:
Column 1: Anecdote or moment
Column 2: How it shows collaboration
Column 3: How it shows segregation or resistance.
Present students with this completed sample row if needed for support and guidance:
Anecdote or Moment
How It Shows Collaboration
How It Shows Segregation or Resistance
“Colored Computers” cafeteria sign on the cafeteria table
Together, the women resisted the sign and kept removing it until it finally disappeared for good.
The sign tried to separate Black women, and removing it showed quiet defiance.
Support students in citing and explaining evidence about working conditions and collaboration in Chapter 6.
Language Focus:
Evidence-based explanation
Contrast language
Event-to-idea reasoning
Students point to one text landmark and orally name the event before explaining what it reveals.
Prompt students to use the second and third columns for interpretation, not just copied details.
When students retell the anecdote only, ask “What bigger idea does this moment reveal about Langley?”
You said the sign was there—we can explain that by saying the sign is evidence of segregation in the workplace.
That idea connects to collaboration because the women were still solving problems together even while unfair rules tried to divide them.
This anecdote shows collaboration because ___.
At the same time, it reveals segregation when ___.
This event develops the idea that ___.
Allow students to discuss possible meanings with a partner before writing so they can test ideas aloud in English or a shared home language.
If students copy text into the chart without analysis → Prompt: “Now add the words ‘This shows . . .’ and finish the idea in your own words.”
If students explain only segregation or only teamwork → Prompt: “What is the second true idea in this same moment?”
Student identifies a specific event and connects it to a larger idea.
Student explains both collaboration and segregation/resistance within the same anecdote.
Pulse Check (RI.6.2)
Which statement best explains how the cafeteria sign anecdote develops ideas in Chapter 6?
It is included mainly to prove that cafeteria rules were the most important part of the women’s jobs at Langley.
Incorrect: The anecdote is not mainly about cafeteria rules themselves; it is about what those rules reveal about segregation and belonging.
It is included to show that even while the women collaborated as skilled mathematicians, segregation still shaped their daily lives at Langley.
Correct: This answer explains both sides of the anecdote and shows how one event develops the chapter’s ideas about teamwork and unfair barriers.
It is included to show that the women worked separately and did not rely on one another to solve problems.
Incorrect: The chapter emphasizes teamwork and how the women as a worked together as a group to solve problems.
It is included only to make the chapter more dramatic and does not connect to the author’s larger ideas.
Incorrect: Anecdotes are purposeful choices that develop central ideas about history and experience, not just entertaining details..
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Moving from Detail to Idea
Provide a clear step-by-step routine to help students move from identifying an event to explaining its meaning. Prompt students to complete two sentence starters for each row:
“This moment shows collaboration because ___.”
“This moment shows segregation or resistance because ___.”
Model how to expand a basic response into a stronger explanation:
“The sign was there” → “The sign shows segregation because it separates workers based on race, even though they are doing the same work.”
Require students to explain both columns for each moment to ensure they move beyond listing details to analyzing how the event develops ideas.
Struggling with: Writing complete explanations in the organizer

Allow students to orally explain their thinking to a partner or teacher before writing. Encourage them to record key words first, then build a complete sentence using a frame. Prompt students to revise short responses by adding a “because” clause to clarify their thinking.
Ready for extension
Add a fourth note below one row explaining how the anecdote connects to the unit idea of hidden figures. Compare two anecdotes and explain which one more strongly shows resistance and why.
Part B: Author’s Purpose and Point of View (RI.6.6) (15 minutes)

Students have already identified key moments of collaboration and segregation in Chapter 6. Now, they will use those details to think about why the author included them. This shift helps students move from identifying a central idea to explaining the author’s purpose and point of view.
Think-Pair-Share
Say these directions:
Respond to the questions using evidence from Chapter 6. Then discuss your responses with your partner.
Ask:
What point of view about teamwork is the author conveying through these moments, and how do the examples support it?

The author’s point of view is that teamwork was essential to the women’s success. She supports this by including examples like how they “double-checked one another’s work,” which shows collaboration as a key strength.
Ask:
Why does the author include examples of collaboration alongside segregation, and how does this choice support her purpose?

The author includes both collaboration and segregation to highlight a contrast. By placing these ideas side by side, she emphasizes how unfair the system was while also showing the women’s resilience. This helps advance her purpose of showing both injustice and strength.
Ask:
What does the author want readers to understand about how these women succeeded, and how do specific details help convey that message?

The author wants readers to understand that the women succeeded through both skill and perseverance. She uses details about their teamwork and the discrimination they faced to show that their success was not easy, which strengthens her message about their determination.
Ask:
How do the author’s choices of details shape the reader’s understanding of NASA at the time?

The author shapes the reader’s view by including details about segregation, like separate spaces, along with examples of important scientific work. This combination helps the reader see NASA as both a place of innovation and a place with serious inequality, supporting the author’s critical perspective.
Support students in orally rehearsing and explaining how specific details from their chart reveal the author’s purpose and point of view in Chapter 6.
Language Focus:
Cause/effect and reasoning language (because, this shows, this helps the reader see)
Author’s purpose language (the author shows, the author wants the reader to understand)
Precise academic nouns (collaboration, segregation, discrimination, resistance)
Students rehearse one response to a Think–Pair–Share question aloud with a partner before sharing.
Encourage students to move beyond describing the moment to explaining why the author included it.
If students only retell the event, prompt them to name what the reader learns from it.
If students give general ideas, guide them back to specific evidence from their chart.
You said they worked together—we can make that clearer by saying this detail shows collaboration because they checked each other’s work.
That connects to author’s purpose because the author includes this moment to show how teamwork helped them succeed despite challenges.
The author shows ___ because ___.
This detail helps the reader understand ___.
The author includes this moment to show ___.
This makes the reader see ___ about NASA/the women.
Provide structured partner talk time so students can practice explaining their thinking out loud before sharing with the class, building confidence with academic language.
If students summarize but do not explain purpose → Prompt: “Why does the author want us to see this? What does the reader learn?”
If students give opinions without evidence → Prompt: “Which moment from your chart shows that? Add a detail.”
Student explains an idea about the text and connects it to the author’s purpose.
Student uses at least one specific detail from their chart to support their thinking.
Student clearly explains what the reader learns from the included details.

Struggling with: Drafting the Explanation

Offer this frame: “In the anecdote about ___, the women show collaboration because ___. At the same time, the scene reveals segregation or resistance when ___. Shetterly includes this moment to ___.” Written Output: Allow students to provide an oral recording of their response or use speech-to-text tools before copying a final version into their Student Edition or Journal.
Ready for extension

Revise the two-to-three-sentence response into one compound-complex sentence plus one follow-up sentence explaining the author's purpose. Add a sentence connecting the anecdote to the broader idea of why some scientific contributors became hidden figures.

Part B: Author’s Purpose and Point of View (RI.6.6)

Quick Write
Say these directions:
For your
Check for Understanding

, use at least two specific details from Chapter 6 to explain the author’s point of view about the women of West Computing. Then briefly analyze how Shetterly uses an anecdote or pattern of events to advance that point of view. Be sure to use at least one contrast connector (such as but, although, or however) in your response.

Shetterly’s point of view is that the women of West Computing were highly skilled collaborators, even as segregation shaped their daily lives. For example, she describes how the women worked together to solve complex math problems and “double-checked one another’s work,” which highlights their teamwork. However, the cafeteria sign “COLORED COMPUTERS” shows that segregation still limited where they could go. By placing these details in contrast, Shetterly emphasizes both their professional excellence and the injustice they faced, helping the reader understand her perspective.
Formatively assess students’ ability to cite evidence and explain dual ideas in a short written response.
Read the background information about the poem, Tuskegee.
The poem “Tuskegee” is about
Tuskegee Institute

, a school founded in 1881 in Alabama to educate Black students during a time when opportunities were very limited because of racism and segregation. Students at Tuskegee learned both academic subjects and practical skills, like building and engineering, to help improve their lives and communities.
Read and annotate Chapter 7 of
Hidden Figures
and the poem,“Tuskegee”. Note any shared idea or similarities in how the authors approach the topic.

standards.description: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text (e.g., through examples or anecdotes).
Determine an author’s point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
Use the relationship between particular words (e.g., cause/effect, part/whole, item/category) to better understand each of the words.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations using appropriate register (e.g., to reflect on multiple perspectives) using a variety of learned phrases, indirect reported speech (e.g., I heard you say X, and Gabriel just pointed out Y), as well as open responses.

Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to gain and hold the floor or ask for clarification) using basic learned phrases (e.g., I think..., Would you please repeat that?), as well as open responses.
Negotiate with or persuade others in conversations (e.g., to provide counterarguments) using an expanded set of learned phrases (I agree with X, but...), as well as open responses.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with light support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with substantial support.

Explain ideas, phenomena, processes, and text relationships (e.g., compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution) based on close reading of a variety of grade‐level texts and viewing of multimedia, with moderate support.

Combine clauses in a wide variety of ways (e.g., creating compound and complex sentences) to make connections between and join ideas, for example, to express a reason (e.g., He stayed at home on Sunday to study for Monday’s exam), to make a concession (e.g., She studied all night even though she wasn’t feeling well), or to link two ideas that happen at the same time (e.g., The students worked in groups while their teacher walked around the room).
Combine clauses in a few basic ways to make connections between and join ideas (e.g., creating compound sentences using and, but, so).

Combine clauses in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., creating compound and complex sentences) to make connections between and join ideas, for example, to express a reason (e.g., He stayed at home on Sunday to study for Monday’s exam) or to make a concession (e.g., She studied all night even though she wasn’t feeling well).
